articles.title: भारत के 57% जिलों में रेड अलर्ट, अल नीनो से पड़ेगी भीषण गर्मी; 75% आबादी पर मंडराया खतरा - Jagran

articles.full_text:
भारत के 57% जिलों में रेड अलर्ट, अल नीनो से पड़ेगी भीषण गर्मी; 75% आबादी पर मंडराया खतरा
अल नीनो के मजबूत होने से दक्षिण एशिया में भीषण गर्मी का खतरा बढ़ गया है, जिसके चलते भारत समेत चारों देशों ने हीट एक्शन प्लान बनाए हैं।
HighLights
अल नीनो से दक्षिण एशिया में भीषण गर्मी का खतरा बढ़ा
हीट एक्शन प्लान को स्वास्थ्य सेवाओं और स्थानीय बजट से जोड़ना चुनौती
भारत के 57% जिले उच्च गर्मी जोखिम में, बड़ी आबादी प्रभावित
संजीव गुप्ता, नई दिल्ली। पूरे प्रशांत महासागर में मजबूत हो रहे अल नीनो के बीच दक्षिण एशिया में भीषण गर्मी का खतरा बढ़ रहा है।
भारत, बांग्लादेश, नेपाल और भूटान ने गर्मी से निपटने के लिए हीट एक्शन प्लान और पूर्व चेतावनी प्रणालियां तो तैयार कर ली हैं, लेकिन अब चुनौती इन व्यवस्थाओं को स्वास्थ्य सेवाओं, स्थानीय बजट और जमीनी स्तर की सुरक्षा से जोड़ने की है।
गुरुवार को ग्लोबल हीट फोरम में चारों देशों के लिए गर्मी और स्वास्थ्य पर पहले राष्ट्र-स्तरीय आकलन जारी किए गए। ये आकलन ग्लोबल हीट हेल्थ इंफॉर्मेशन नेटवर्क-साउथ एशिया हब के पहले आकलन हैं, जिसकी मेजबानी नई दिल्ली स्थित काउंसिल ऑन एनर्जी, एनवायरनमेंट एंड वाटर (सीईईडब्ल्यू) कर रहा है।
भारत में 57 प्रतिशत जिले उच्च से बहुत उच्च गर्मी जोखिम में
सीईईडब्ल्यू के जिला-स्तरीय अध्ययन के अनुसार, भारत के 57 प्रतिशत जिले पहले से ही गर्मी के उच्च से बहुत उच्च जोखिम का सामना कर रहे हैं। इन जिलों में देश की करीब तीन-चौथाई आबादी रहती है।
भारत में 250 से अधिक शहर और जिला स्तरीय हीट एक्शन प्लान लागू हैं। लू को आपदा जोखिम प्रबंधन कोष के तहत अधिसूचित प्राकृतिक आपदा के रूप में मान्यता दी जा चुकी है।
गर्मी से होने वाली बीमारियों की राष्ट्रीय निगरानी व्यवस्था भी बनाई गई है और 18,000 से अधिक मेडिकल ऑफिसरों को प्रशिक्षण दिया गया है।
आकलन में कहा गया है कि अब गर्मी से निपटने की कार्रवाई को सिर्फ आपदा प्रबंधन तक सीमित रखने के बजाय इसके लिए अलग फंड और हर योजना में स्वास्थ्य से जुड़े नतीजों को शामिल करने की जरूरत है।
नेपाल में 2024 में 50 दिन 40 डिग्री से ऊपर तापमान
हिमालयी देश नेपाल में भीषण गर्मी का जोखिम तेजी से उभर रहा है। राष्ट्रीय मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 2024 में दक्षिणी तराई के मैदानों में 50 दिन तापमान 40 डिग्री सेल्सियस से ऊपर रहा।
नेपाल ने अपनी पहली संघीय हीट योजना जारी करने के साथ चरणबद्ध हीट अलर्ट प्रणाली शुरू की है। हालांकि, स्वास्थ्य व्यवस्था में गर्मी से होने वाली बीमारियों के आंकड़े अभी व्यवस्थित तरीके से दर्ज नहीं किए जाते।
आकलन में तराई के अस्पतालों में गर्मी के कारण भर्ती होने वाले मरीजों की अनिवार्य रिकॉर्डिंग शुरू करने और मौसम विभाग की चेतावनियों को जमीनी कार्रवाई तक पहुंचाने की व्यवस्था मजबूत करने का सुझाव दिया गया है।
बांग्लादेश में साल का एक-तिहाई हिस्सा खतरनाक उमस भरी गर्मी
विश्व बैंक के अनुसार, बांग्लादेश में 1980 से अब तक महसूस होने वाले तापमान में करीब 4.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस की वृद्धि हुई है। अब साल का लगभग एक-तिहाई हिस्सा खतरनाक उमस भरी गर्मी वाला होता है।
बांग्लादेश ने अपनी राष्ट्रीय अनुकूलन योजना में गर्मी को शामिल किया है और नारायणगंज में पहला शहरी हीट एक्शन प्लान बनाया है। गर्मी से जुड़ी बीमारियों पर राष्ट्रीय दिशानिर्देश जारी करने के साथ ‘बी.ई.ए.टी. द हीट’ नाम से जन अभियान भी शुरू किया गया है।
आकलन में राष्ट्रीय और उप-राष्ट्रीय स्तर पर अलग-अलग हीट एक्शन प्लान तथा अस्पतालों को राष्ट्रीय पूर्वानुमानों से जोड़ने वाली गर्मी-स्वास्थ्य निगरानी प्रणाली की जरूरत बताई गई है।
भूटान में ठंडी घाटियों तक पहुंच रहा गर्मी का जोखिम
भूटान के दक्षिणी निचले इलाकों में बढ़ती गर्मी अब उन घाटियों को भी अधिक तापमान की ओर धकेल रही है, जहां पहले भीषण गर्मी से बचाव की योजनाओं की जरूरत नहीं पड़ती थी।
राष्ट्रीय स्तर के निर्देशों में गर्मी से जुड़ी जिम्मेदारियां स्वास्थ्य मंत्रालय को दी गई हैं। 2022 के एक नियम में श्रमिकों को गर्मी से सुरक्षा देना अनिवार्य किया गया है।
भूटान के पास बाढ़ और ग्लेशियर झीलों के लिए पहले से पूर्व चेतावनी प्रणालियां हैं। आकलन में इन व्यवस्थाओं के आधार पर गर्मी से निपटने के लिए एकीकृत हीट एक्शन प्लान बनाने का सुझाव दिया गया है।
चारों देशों में तैयारी बढ़ी, लेकिन जमीनी कार्रवाई में अंतर
आकलनों के मुताबिक, चारों देशों में गर्मी से निपटने की तैयारियों ने रफ्तार पकड़ी है। हीट एक्शन प्लान और पूर्वानुमान एवं पूर्व चेतावनी प्रणालियां योजना और नीति के स्तर पर सबसे तेजी से आगे बढ़ी हैं।
अब स्वास्थ्य निगरानी, स्थानीय कार्रवाई के लिए वित्तपोषण और स्वास्थ्य, श्रम तथा शहरी नियोजन में गर्मी को शामिल करने जैसी व्यवस्थाओं को मजबूत करने की जरूरत है। यही व्यवस्थाएं मौसम संबंधी चेतावनी को वास्तविक जमीनी सुरक्षा में बदल सकती हैं।
‘हर चेतावनी को भरोसेमंद सुरक्षा में बदलना होगा’
सीईईडब्ल्यू के फेलो और साउथ एशिया हब के अध्यक्ष डॉ. विश्वास चितले ने कहा कि दक्षिण एशिया में भीषण गर्मी अब पूरे साल बनी रहने वाला क्षेत्रीय जोखिम बन चुकी है। उनके अनुसार, क्षेत्र शून्य से शुरुआत नहीं कर रहा है और प्रत्येक देश ने पांच साल पहले की तुलना में गर्मी की स्थिति खराब होने का अनुमान लगाया है।
उन्होंने कहा कि अब इन पूर्वानुमानों को स्वास्थ्य व्यवस्थाओं, स्थानीय बजट और श्रम नियमों से जोड़ने की जरूरत है, ताकि हर चेतावनी को भरोसेमंद तरीके से सुरक्षा में बदला जा सके।

articles.title: Mumbai's 1st post-monsoon heatwave warning: Mercury hits 37.6°C, ; yellow alert for Oct 9 - The Times of India

articles.full_text:
MUMBAI: Mumbai has barely had time to bid goodbye to the monsoon and the city is already staring at its first heatwave warning of the post-monsoon season.
The
India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Thursday issued a yellow alert for a heatwave in isolated pockets of Mumbai and Raigad for October 9, as temperatures continued to hover several degrees above normal.
The warning comes just six days after the IMD announced the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon from Mumbai on October 3, an unusually swift shift from monsoon conditions to heatwave-like weather.
On Thursday, the IMD also declared the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon from the entire state of Maharashtra.
Mumbai’s Santacruz observatory recorded a maximum temperature of 37.6°C on Thursday, 4.5°C above normal, while Colaba recorded 36.5°C, 3.9°C above normal. The Thane-Belapur belt was also hot, recording a maximum of 37.2°C.
The jump has been particularly sharp. Just a day earlier, the maximum temperatures at Colaba and Santacruz were 34°C and 35.4°C respectively.
For Mumbai and other coastal areas, the IMD’s heatwave criteria take into account both the absolute temperature and its departure from normal.
A heatwave is declared when the maximum temperature reaches at least 37°C and is 4.5°C or more above normal for two consecutive days.
The 37.6°C recorded at Santacruz on Thursday was also the highest October temperature recorded at the observatory in eight years. The highest October maximum last year was 37°C, recorded on October 17.
The October peak temperatures at Santacruz in recent years were 36.5°C in 2025, 37.4°C in 2024, 37.4°C in 2023, 35.4°C in 2022, 36.4°C in 2021, 35°C in 2020 and 36.6°C in 2019.
At Colaba too, Thursday’s 36.5°C was the highest October maximum since the year 2019. The observatory had recorded 37.2°C in October 2018.
Despite the scorching afternoons, minimum temperatures have not shown a similar spike. Santacruz recorded a minimum of 24.7°C on Thursday, close to normal, while Colaba recorded 26.5°C, 1.1°C above normal. Relative humidity remained high at 78% at Santacruz and 89% at Colaba, adding to the discomfort.
The city’s October record highs, however, remain some distance away. Colaba’s highest October maximum is 39.5°C, recorded on October 22, 1968, while Santacruz’s October record stands at 38.6°C, recorded on October 17, 2015.
Weather experts expect the hot spell to continue through October 14 or possibly into the middle of next week.
Independent weather observer Abhijit Modak said the current weather pattern was particularly favourable for a sharp rise in daytime temperatures.
Modak said, “The combination of a persistent high-pressure area over Gujarat and easterly to northeasterly winds is currently suppressing the sea breeze over Konkan, allowing temperatures to rise sharply during the day. Mumbai and parts of the MMR could therefore see temperatures approach 39°C in the coming days."
"The early withdrawal of the monsoon, below-normal rainfall in September and the lack of a significant post-monsoon thunderstorm spell have further reduced moisture and cloud cover, allowing the land surface to heat up quickly. With these conditions likely to persist, the first half of October could remain unusually hot, with temperatures potentially peaking around October 14,” he added.

articles.title: Bangladesh, 3 other South Asian countries launch new initiative to tackle extreme heat - Prothom Alo English

articles.full_text:
The El Niño phenomenon is strengthening across the Pacific, increasing the risk of another season of extreme heat in South Asia.
Against this backdrop, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Bhutan have launched a joint initiative to tackle the impacts of extreme heat.
Four new country briefs assessing heatwave conditions, preparedness and gaps in the four countries were released today, Thursday, at the Global Heat Forum, which began in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, says a press release.
The briefs were published under the initiative of the South Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN). The assessments were conducted as part of a review of countries’ preparedness and capacity as health risks from extreme heat continue to rise across South Asia. They examine how the countries are responding to extreme heat, preparing in advance and where significant gaps remain.
The Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) in New Delhi runs the South Asia Hub. Its partners include the Sustainable Futures Collaborative, Natural Resources Defense Council, BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health, and the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP). The initiative is also aligned with the joint climate and health programme of the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
Heatwaves in South Asia have become more intense and longer in recent years. Extreme heat causes more than discomfort; it poses serious health risks, particularly for children, older people, pregnant women and outdoor workers. In addition to heat-related illness and deaths, extreme heat can increase the risks of heart disease, respiratory illnesses and other health problems.
The purpose of the new assessments of the four countries is to identify areas where progress has been made in addressing heat-related health risks and where more coordinated action is needed. The findings could be used in policymaking, strengthening health systems, early warning systems and protecting vulnerable populations.
The Global Heat Forum in Bangkok is discussing the growing risk of extreme heat and its health impacts in South Asia and other regions around the world. Experts have warned that climate change could further increase the risk of heatwaves in the future. As a result, there is growing emphasis on treating heat not simply as a weather event but as a major public health risk.
In Bangladesh, the feels-like temperature, which takes both temperature and humidity into account, has risen by about 4.5°C since 1980. People now spend nearly one-third of the year in dangerously humid heat.
Heat has been recognised as a risk in Bangladesh’s National Adaptation Plan. The country’s first urban heatwave action plan has been developed for Narayanganj. National guidelines for dealing with heat-related illness and a public awareness campaign called “Beat the Heat” have also been launched.
Despite these initiatives, however, there is a lack of dedicated heatwave action plans at both national and local levels. It is also important to establish a system for monitoring heat-related illness by linking weather forecasts with hospitals and the health system.
These findings and recommendations are included in the first Bangladesh assessment by the South Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN). Four separate assessments of heat and health conditions in Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Bhutan were released today, Thursday, at the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok, Thailand.
First assessments of the four countries
This is the first assessment by the GHHIN South Asia Hub of heat and health risks in the four countries.
At the time of the release, it was announced that El Niño is strengthening in the Pacific, which could increase the risk of another season of extreme heat in South Asia. Against this backdrop, Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Bhutan have begun working together to address the impacts of extreme heat.
Plans have advanced, but implementation remains a challenge
The assessment of the four countries says preparations for tackling heat in South Asia have progressed most rapidly in the areas of planning, weather forecasting and early warning. All four countries have developed heatwave action plans and early warning systems in one form or another.
However, measures to translate these plans and warnings into protection on the ground have not advanced at the same pace. Major gaps remain in monitoring heat-related illness, financing local-level initiatives, and integrating heat risks into health, labour and urban planning. While several countries have begun large-scale initiatives, progress is uneven.
Extreme heat was once mainly seen in the plains of South Asia. It is now spreading to the Himalayan countries of Nepal and Bhutan as well.
Health risks in Bangladesh remain under-recognised
Farzana Misha of the BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health said, “Heat is one of the least recognised health risks in this region. It is less visible than floods or cyclones. But its impacts on health, work and food security are no less serious. In Bangladesh, we have already started taking some initiatives. A national guideline for dealing with heat-related illness and the country’s first urban heatwave action plan in Narayanganj have been developed. Similar initiatives are being undertaken in Dhaka, Rajshahi and other urban centres. Now similar action is needed across South Asia. We need to build health systems and provide the necessary financing so that risks can be identified before the heat arrives and action can be taken before people are affected.”
The Bangladesh assessment recommends developing dedicated heatwave action plans at both national and local levels. It also calls for establishing a system to monitor heat and health by linking the country’s weather forecasts with hospitals.
India has made the most progress
Among the four countries, India has made the most progress in shifting from reactive relief measures to anticipatory action to reduce heat risks.
District-level research by CEEW found that 57 per cent of India’s districts are at high or very high risk of extreme heat. Nearly three-quarters of the country’s population live in these districts.
More than 250 heatwave action plans are in place at the city and district levels in India. Heatwaves have also been officially recognised as a natural disaster under the country’s disaster risk management financing framework. A national system for monitoring heat-related illness has been established, and more than 18,000 medical officers have been trained.
However, the assessment recommends taking India’s heat action plans beyond the boundaries of disaster management. It calls for dedicated financing and systems to assess health outcomes to be included in every plan.
Nepal experienced 50 days of temperatures above 40°C
Nepal, a Himalayan country, has traditionally faced floods, droughts and other water- and weather-related disasters. It is now also facing the risk of extreme heat.
According to data from Nepal’s national meteorological department, temperatures in the country’s southern Terai plains exceeded 40°C for 50 days in 2024.
Nepal has already published its first national heatwave action plan and issues risk-based warnings. However, the country’s health system does not yet routinely record data on heat-related illness.
The assessment recommends making it mandatory for hospitals in the Terai region to record admissions related to extreme heat. It also calls for strengthening the process of ensuring that weather warnings reach local communities and that appropriate action is taken accordingly.
Heat is rising even in Bhutan’s cooler valleys
Bhutan’s southern lowlands are becoming warmer. As a result, temperatures are also rising in valleys that were previously cooler. Communities that had never before needed to plan for extreme heat are now at risk.
Bhutan’s national policy assigns responsibility for tackling heat to the Ministry of Health. A 2022 regulation also requires measures to protect workers from heat.
Bhutan has relatively advanced early warning systems for floods and glacial lake outburst disasters. The assessment says these systems could also be expanded to cover heat. It recommends bringing different policies and responsibilities together to develop an integrated national heatwave action plan.
Forecasts must be turned into protection
Biswas Chitale, a fellow at CEEW and chair of the GHHIN South Asia Hub, said extreme heat is now a year-round regional risk in South Asia.
However, the region does not have to start from scratch in tackling the risk. Every country is projected to experience worse heat conditions than five years ago.
According to Chitale, the key task now is to link weather forecasts with health systems, local budgets and labour regulations. A warning must be turned into effective protection for people.
Kyeong Ko, director of the Information and Communication Technology and Disaster Risk Reduction Division at UNESCAP, said heat does not stop at borders. Therefore, responses to it should not be confined within national borders either. Countries can share forecasts, coordinate temperature thresholds for taking action and incorporate heat risks into existing disaster management systems.
Following the Global Heat Forum, the South Asia Hub will develop a regional network and training programme involving various organisations. Situation assessments will also be prepared for the governments of the four countries before and after the heat season. The goal will be to turn scientific information on heat into coordinated action and ensure the protection of the region’s most vulnerable populations.

Weather cools further in Tricity as yellow alert shifts to weekend
Chandigarh cools to 31.2°C, Panchkula records Haryana’s lowest temperature; IMD forecasts rain, thunderstorms through Oct 13.
The yellow alert for thunderstorms, lightning and strong gusty winds issued for Thursday passed without any significant impact in the Chandigarh Tricity till the filing of this report, a day after brief showers brought relief from the heat.
The weather remained comparatively cooler on Thursday, with an overcast sky and cool breeze keeping daytime temperatures down further.
Chandigarh recorded a maximum temperature of 31.2°C, 1.7°C lower than Wednesday and 0.9°C below normal. The minimum temperature also fell by 2°C to 22.2°C, though it remained 2.9°C above normal. The city received no fresh rain during the day after recording 7.8 mm in the preceding 24 hours.
Panchkula remained the coolest of the three Tricity cities as well as the coolest in Haryana, recording a maximum of 29.7°C and a minimum of 20.4°C. The maximum and minimum temperatures were 2.1°C and 1.8°C lower than the previous day and night, respectively. Both were the lowest among the reported temperatures in Haryana.
Panchkula had received 16 mm of rain in the preceding 24 hours, but no fresh rainfall was recorded between 8.30 am and 5.30 pm on Thursday.
Mohali also turned cooler, with the maximum temperature falling to 31.3°C, 2°C lower than Wednesday. The minimum dropped to 22.7°C, down 1°C from the previous night. No rain was recorded in Mohali during the observation period.
The cooling was more pronounced during the day, with maximum temperatures across the Tricity now below normal. Nights, however, continued to remain warmer than normal.
Humidity also rose sharply in Chandigarh, adding to the moisture-laden feel despite the cooler temperatures. Relative humidity ranged from 59 per cent to 96 per cent, with the maximum touching 96 per cent.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has eased the immediate thunderstorm warning while retaining the possibility of weather activity over the weekend. Isolated rain or thunderstorm activity is forecast across Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh through October 13.
For the Tricity, maximum temperatures are expected to remain around 30°C on Friday, 29°C on Saturday, 30°C on Sunday, 31°C on Monday and 32°C on Tuesday. Minimum temperatures are likely to remain around 22°C throughout.
The change in weather comes after Wednesday’s brief spell of rain, which broke the preceding dry spell and brought a marked fall in daytime temperatures across the Tricity.

There’s nothing like an election to get the blood flowing and the political promises moving. Such is the case when it comes to small business in the province.
Several consequential promises have landed in the campaign so far.
BC NDP leader David Eby said his re-elected government would offer interest-free loans of up to $1 million to small and medium-sized businesses affected by the U.S. trade war and rising costs. The loans would be good for up to 72 months.
“These interest-free loans will provide the support that the small and medium-sized business leaders have come to us and said they need to be able to get through this period, and our commitment is that we will deliver that for them,” said Eby.
It’s long been a request from the business community to get some sort of government backstop for the small businesses sitting precariously on the edge of the trade war. But it’s taken almost two years for the governing party to move on the issue, and only during a campaign.
BC NDP promise tax credit for youth hires
Similarly, business leaders like the Canadian Federation of Independent Business have been urging government to create incentives for business owners to hire youth. British Columbia and Saskatchewan are two of the only provinces without tax credits and wage subsidizing to make it easier to hire young people and get them experience in the workforce. It comes at a time of high youth unemployment, and concerns expressed by political leaders like Eby that temporary foreign workers are cheaper and easier for some businesses to hire than local youth.
Eby promised a $5,000 refundable tax credit for youth hires for small businesses on Wednesday.
“This money will help small businesses bring on employees, and will provide an opportunity for a young person to get that first job, to get into the job market, to get that experience,” he said.
It moves B.C. in line with Manitoba, and ahead of Ontario, in youth employment incentives, which the CFIB praised Wednesday.
Still, the election campaign has also frozen some critical business policies mid-stream.
Election delays long-awaited food production changes
The multi-year campaign to get B.C. to open up more food production on protected Agricultural Land Reserve property was on the verge of becoming a reality prior to the early writ drop in September. The government was just wrapping up extended consultation, before Eby plunged voters into an early election.
Now, new federal funding has opened up for food processors at a time when the B.C. government is caught mid-stream in changes. Eby tried to brush aside the impact.
“We had the farmers ask for a little bit more time to do engagement on that with their members and provide feedback to us as government,” he said. “That will conclude this month, and then we’ll be in a position to make any changes.”
If he wins re-election, that is.
In the meantime, the farming sector is stuck with prohibitive rules at a time when Ottawa is funnelling critical cash out the door.
BC Conservatives will cut PST on new investments in businesses
On the BC Conservative side, leader Lorne Doerkson offered up a long-requested change to drop the Provincial Sales Tax on capital inputs for businesses.
The PST is an archaic tax, embedding itself again and again on machinery, equipment and other items businesses buy on the road to making a product or service. Since B.C. backed out of the Harmonized Sales Tax in 2013, the business community has been asking for the PST input exemption to improve competitiveness.
“Right now, when a local business buys the equipment its workers need, the seven per cent PST acts as a direct penalty on that growth,” said Doerkson.
“We are eliminating the PST on more business investments in machinery, tools, and software for a three-year period. This will absolutely give B.C. businesses a very massive incentive to invest in their businesses and help us supercharge the B.C. economy. That is our plan. It is to supercharge our economy.”
The Conservatives did not immediately disclose the cost of the PST input holiday.
The NDP said their interest-free loan program is worth $500 million — most of which, presumably, would be paid back by the businesses over three years.
The two parties have sparred over how each other’s promises would be funded, with both pledging to release fully-costed platforms later in the campaign.
Greens unveil ‘green industrial strategy’
The BC Greens, mostly free of having to cost their platform, but also fuelled by a proposed wealth tax on people with more than $50 million that it says could generate more than $22 billion, have a different set of promises on business.
Leader Emily Lowan has called for a wholesale shift in government, to use its purchasing power to support local businesses and build regional economies. It’s part of an “economic vision” for the province the Greens released Wednesday that promised to “develop a green industrial strategy that coordinates electricity, infrastructure, skills, financing, research and public procurement around areas where B.C. has the ingredients to build lasting industries and good jobs.”
The Greens have virtually no chance of being able to directly implement their ideas in a government. But they could, once again, hold the balance of power in a deadlocked legislature if the current trajectory of a close race continues. Which makes their platform worth reading in the business community.
In the meantime, at only the half way point of the election, expect more promises to start flying as more voters turn their mind to advanced voting that begins Oct. 16.

Morocco’s General Directorate of Meteorology has issued an orange-level weather alert for thunderstorms, hail and strong wind gusts expected across 23 provinces on Thursday.
The storms are forecast to bring rainfall of between 20 and 30 millimeters in affected areas, according to an updated warning issued Thursday, Oct. 8.
The alert covers the provinces of Taza, Figuig, Youssoufia, Ouarzazate, Driouch, Al Haouz, Tata, Boulemane, Midelt, Errachidia, Khouribga, El Kelaa des Sraghna, Marrakech, Rhamna, Beni Mellal, Azilal, Chichaoua, Zagora, Tinghir, Taroudant, Fquih Ben Salah, Nador and Guercif.
The thunderstorms are expected to begin at noon and continue until 11 p.m. Thursday, the meteorological service said.
Hail and strong wind gusts are also possible locally, with rainfall totals expected to reach 30 mm in some areas.
The warning reflects the potential for significant weather disturbances in the affected areas during the specified period.
